title: 'The internet is here': emergent coordination and innovation of protest forms in digital culture
text:
ʻThe Internet is Hereʼ: Emergent Coordination and Innovation of Protest Forms in Digital Culture Patrick Underwood Department of Sociology University of Washington Seattle, WA 98105 patriu@u.washington.edu

Howard T. Welser Department of Sociology Ohio University Athens, Ohio 45701 welser@ohio.edu

ABSTRACT The series of protests against the Church of Scientology known as “Project Chanology” marks the emergence of an important form of contemporary protest movement defined by networked internal structures and pervasive memetic culture. Such a protest movement is highly dynamic- rapidly adapting to changing challenges and contextual settings. This cultural innovation is made possible by the increasing digital mediation of social life. In the following analysis, we trace the unique structural contours of Chanology, investigate how participants leveraged a unique internal structure and the memetic environment of the internet to grow, and conclude with an explanation of why the novel modes of protest used in Chanology contributed to its success and why these forms of protest are likely to proliferate in an increasingly digitally mediated environment. From a theoretical standpoint, Project Chanology both affirms and challenges conventional conceptions of social movements. The utility of Chwe’s network analytical approach to the problems of coordination in social movements is also demonstrated.

Categories and Subject Descriptors A.0 [General Literature]: General – Conference proceedings.

General Terms Human Factors, Theory.

Keywords 
Culture, social movements, protest, memes, Chanology, 
networked activism. 

1. INTRODUCTION On February 10th 2008, approximately 10,000 individuals from the loosely affiliated online collective known as Anonymous gathered in cities around the world to engage in coordinated

protests against the Church of Scientology. These protests delivered a mixture of serious accusations of fraud and human rights abuses at the hands of the Church within a playful, carnivalesque, and at times obscure atmosphere. What was perhaps most remarkable about these protests was that they were carried out by a decentralized group with no formal leadership or internal organizational structures. The following analysis draws upon qualitative and quantitative observations of public sites on which participants involved in Project Chanology interacted. We begin with an examination of the defining cultural and structural characteristics of Project Chanology, paying close attention to the ways in which the group leveraged online communications technologies and its memetic culture. Next, we move to an examination of why Project Chanology was initially successful and how it was able to expand by drawing in new participants. We draw upon a theory of emergent cultural coordination in low density networks [12] to aid in an explanation of how the structure of Chanology was of great utility in rapid coordination of group action. Finally, we explore how the novel aspects of Chanology contributed to its success and demonstrate the utility of these new forms of protest in contemporary social movement activism.

2. LITERATURE REVIEW 2.1 Social Interaction in a Connected Age Online and off, social groups are changing [4], [31], [34], [35]. The things that we do today, how we do them, and with whom have shifted in recent years. Just five years ago it was rare to post messages or images from a cell phone. Now, hand held social computing is nearly ubiquitous and being connected is the default condition for young adults [29]. The more that people interact online, the more that our communities, our culture, our groups and our identities are shaped by dynamics of computer mediated interaction. As modes of social interaction (Facebook, YouTube, Flickr, etc.) become increasingly rich it becomes easier for online culture to bleed into what William Gibson dubbed the “meatspace”, and for events from the “meatspace” to reverberate back into the computer mediated world. Clay Shirky remarked that technology becomes socially interesting when it becomes technologically boring [34]. He meant that when computer mediated interaction becomes common enough, that it changes the inherent “friction” that prevents people from doing things together [41]. We interact differently online than we do in face to face life. Like industrialization moving people from small towns to the metropolis [36], online interaction

2.2 Social Movements Social movements are a basic foundation of contemporary democratic societies [26], [40]. They provide outlets for political positions to be voiced, for powerful actors to be critiqued, and for grievances to be aired [28]. Although people participate in movements for many reasons, a crucial foundation is identity commitment, or people’s capacity to see the values and practices embodied in social movement organizations as fundamental to their definition of self [28], [37]. Project Chanology represents in interesting instance in which identity commitment appears to be centered on having fun and the image of the self as trickster. Social movements employ a host of strategies, techniques, and tactical repertoires [39], [40]. At any given point, a movement has a repertoire of protest forms at its disposal, and will employ some organic set of strategies from those apparent to movement participants [38]. This is true of social movements using online technologies as well [33]. Throughout history, social movements have adopted strategies demonstrated by earlier movements and have innovated new strategies to confront new challenges, types of opponents, or novel situations [27], [40].

2.3 Computer Mediated Interaction, Memes and Innovation of New Forms of Social Protest The rise of new participatory types of computer mediated interaction (CMI) increases peoples’ capacity to organize in social movements. Ubiquitous CMI also changes the structure of interaction between the social movement participants and others. The audience for movement participants is larger and more diverse when anyone can post a video to YouTube, comment on a blog, or recommend a link to a social new aggregation site like Reddit or Digg. Given the right set of images or situation, the next internet meme can come from anywhere, and when cultural objects “go viral” they change the terrain of those involved, and can alter the opportunity structure for future events. Memes [16] are distinctive cultural objects that are transmitted through communication, and spread through a population of social actors in a manner analogous to the spread of viruses through a population of organisms. Online, the term meme is also used to describe inside jokes and clichés employed in online communities like 4chan, Digg, Icanhazcheezeburger, etc. Finally, the diffusion of innovations through interpersonal communication has long been a subject of social scientific research, and especially in the context of social movements. Social movements require tactics and modes of protest, and these movement options themselves are subject to dynamics of innovation and diffusion. All three conceptualizations of how ideas spread become relevant to the social movement dynamics of Chanology. Ron Burt notes that many examples of “innovation” involve brokering, or actions that bridge between otherwise unconnected communities [10], [11]. Because culture is growing so rapidly, and in such complexly interconnected directions, we should expect that culture, in terms of practices, values, and sensibilities that emerge in one context, may well be carried into new social terrain. The case of Chanology illustrates how culture, internet memes, and the social role of the internet troll led to the innovation of new forms of social protest. An analysis of Chanology extends our growing awareness and understanding of new modes of social interaction emerging alongside the increasing proliferation of online communications technologies.

3. DATA For the present analysis, we draw upon two primary sources of data. The first is comprised of empirical observation of the public, online sources used by members of Anonymous to plan, discuss, coordinate, and execute Project Chanology. When making these observations we focused less on discussion of Scientology and more upon how the participants saw themselves and the various rhetorical strategies employed to sustain group interaction and to build consensus. The second source of data is drawn from a quantitative analysis of interactions amongst Project Chanology participants at a wiki site. We constructed a network representing communication amongst individuals and also built measures of integration within the broader community at the site, which was used for more than just Chanology. While the data are not perfect and do not permit a view of the totality of Project Chanology taken together, they permit an examination of group structure as well as the myriad cultural, contextual factors that shaped Project Chanology.

4. ANALYSIS 4.1 Part 1: Structural and Cultural Features 4.1.1 Decentralization Interaction amongst members of Anonymous participating in Project Chanology was of a highly decentralized and networked quality. Within the group, we did not find evidence of official leadership positions or formal organizational structures. In fact we commonly observed strong hostility towards those attempting to single handedly guide the actions of other participants. Such individuals were commonly derisively referred to as “leaderfags.” Over time, a geographically-based cell structure developed and duties within cells were assumed in an ad-hoc, volunteer based manner. In one instance that typified the assumption of such duties we noted an individual that claimed to work in the field of graphic design offering his or her expertise in designing graphics for protest signs. In another instance one participant, referring to the need for bringing water to a protest stated “Well soemone (sic) has to do it, might as well be me.” Decisions impacting Chanology as a whole were primarily made through consensus building and collaborative interaction at specific websites and IRC channels. This collaborative structure allowed the group to work rapidly and democratically. This also made the overall group more resilient against the effects of individuals leaving and ensured that there were no easy or obvious targets for retaliation from Scientology. Finally, this structure encouraged the development of highly dynamic and emergent strategies as many individuals with varying ideas and talents were able to work simultaneously on a given project. Many explicitly recognized this advantage. One forum had a subsection dedicated to individuals listing skills and talents which might be of use.

4.1.2 The Centrality of Humor and Memes One of the most distinctive aspects of Project Chanology was the pervasiveness and importance of humor and memetic knowledge
